title: Microsoft Azure Administrator — concise course notes

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Cloud Shell provides an authenticated browser command line for managing Azure resources with Bash or PowerShell.

lessons.title: What is Azure Cloud Shell?
points: Cloud Shell lets you manage virtual machines, storage and networking without installing Azure command-line tools locally.
Microsoft maintains the Azure CLI and PowerShell modules in the hosted environment.
The shell uses your signed-in account and its existing permissions; opening a shell does not grant additional resource access.
Persist scripts and SSH keys in Cloud Shell storage so that they remain available between sessions.
Use the Cloud Shell editor to change stored scripts directly in the browser.

lessons.title: How does Azure Cloud Shell work?
points: Open Cloud Shell from shell.azure.com, the Azure portal or a supported Microsoft Learn code snippet.
A temporary host is allocated to your session; choose Bash or PowerShell before running commands.
Sessions terminate after 20 minutes of inactivity. Start a new session to continue working.
Files stored on CloudDrive persist after the temporary session ends and can be accessed from another device.
An Azure Files share can be mounted for persistent files; the share is associated with a particular region.
Open the built-in editor from the toolbar or run code <filename> to edit a file.
Cloud Shell includes tools such as Git, Terraform, Ansible, kubectl and Helm, alongside Azure tools.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: use cloud shell editor

lessons.title: When should you use Azure Cloud Shell?
points: Choose Cloud Shell for occasional Azure administration from a browser when your usual workstation is unavailable.
Use persistent storage when you need the same scripts in later sessions.
Avoid relying on a temporary shell session for unattended or long-running work; inactivity can disconnect the session and lose its current state.
Choose your own virtual machine or container when you need administrator privileges or unsupported installed tools.
Cloud Shell has a default limit of 20 concurrent users per tenant; request a quota increase for larger training sessions.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Use Cloud Shell for browser-based administration, and save files in persistent storage rather than relying on the temporary host.

modules.title: Deploy Azure infrastructure by using JSON ARM templates

lessons.title: Introduction
points: ARM templates describe Azure infrastructure declaratively in JSON and can be versioned with application code.
Microsoft recommends Bicep for people starting infrastructure as code on Azure because it offers simpler authoring than JSON templates.

lessons.title: Explore Azure Resource Manager template structure
points: Infrastructure as code keeps resource configuration in version control, making deployments repeatable and changes traceable.
An ARM template declares the desired resources and properties; Resource Manager organizes their creation and dependencies.
Templates are idempotent: repeating an unchanged deployment does not create duplicate resources.
The required template sections include $schema, contentVersion and resources. Optional sections include parameters, variables, functions and outputs.
Parameters supply deployment-specific values; variables simplify expressions; outputs return values after deployment.
Deploy a local template after signing in with az login or Connect-AzAccount and selecting the intended subscription and resource group.
For resource-group deployment, use az deployment group create or New-AzResourceGroupDeployment; review deployment status and history in the portal.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create and deploy an Azure Resource Manager template
points: Create azuredeploy.json in Visual Studio Code with the template schema, version and an initially empty resources section.
Sign in using Azure CLI or PowerShell, select the intended subscription, and create or select the exercise resource group.
Deploy the empty template in the default incremental mode and inspect its successful deployment record; it creates no resources.
Add a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource with its name, API version, location, kind and SKU, then deploy the updated template.
Review the resource and deployment history in the Azure portal. Follow the official exercise in your own chosen lab environment.

lessons.title: Add flexibility to your Azure Resource Manager template by using parameters and outputs
points: Use parameters for values that vary by environment, such as resource names, SKUs, size and capacity.
Define each parameter with a type and optionally a default, allowed values, length or value constraints, and a description.
A template supports up to 256 parameters; supply values on the command line or in a parameter file.
Use secureString for secrets and secureObject for objects containing sensitive values. Do not hardcode secrets or provide secret defaults.
Reference a parameter in a resource with the parameters function, so one template can serve several environments.
Outputs have a declared type and value; the reference function can retrieve runtime resource properties such as storage endpoints.
Redeploying with the same resource names and scopes updates existing resources. In incremental mode, specify all non-default properties because omitted properties can reset to defaults.

lessons.title: Exercise - Add parameters and outputs to your Azure Resource Manager template
points: Add a storageName parameter and use it in the storage account resource name.
Add a storageSKU parameter with an allowedValues list and replace the fixed SKU with the parameter expression.
Deploy with an allowed SKU, then observe that a value outside the allowed list fails validation.
Add a storageEndpoint output using the storage account runtime properties and inspect it in the deployment result and portal.
Follow the official exercise for exact commands and naming requirements; this app does not deploy resources for you.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Parameters make a template reusable across deployments, while outputs expose useful results such as resource endpoints.

paths.title: AZ-104: Manage identities and governance in Azure

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Microsoft Entra ID is a cloud identity and access service for users, applications and devices.

lessons.title: Examine Microsoft Entra ID
points: Microsoft manages the Entra ID directory service; customers do not deploy or maintain its domain controllers.
Use Entra ID for users and groups, application access, single sign-on, multifactor authentication and Conditional Access.
A tenant is an isolated directory instance containing identities and applications.
An Azure subscription is associated with exactly one Entra tenant at a time; the same tenant can serve multiple subscriptions.
A tenant receives an onmicrosoft.com domain and can also use verified custom domain names.
Entra ID does not use the traditional organizational-unit and Group Policy hierarchy of AD DS.
An application object defines an application; a service principal represents that application in a particular tenant.

lessons.title: Compare Microsoft Entra ID and Active Directory Domain Services
points: AD DS is a Windows Server directory with a hierarchical structure, organizational units, Group Policy and domain-joined computers.
AD DS uses LDAP for directory queries and Kerberos for authentication.
Entra ID is designed for internet applications and uses web protocols including SAML, OpenID Connect and OAuth.
Entra users and groups have a flat directory structure; traditional AD DS Group Policy does not apply to them.
Running an AD DS domain controller on an Azure virtual machine is distinct from using Entra ID.
The source recommends extra data disks for AD DS database, logs and SYSVOL on Azure virtual machines, with disk host caching set to None.

lessons.title: Examine Microsoft Entra ID as a directory service for cloud apps
points: A shared Entra tenant can provide identity services for Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and Intune.
Centralized application authentication can give users single sign-on across integrated cloud applications.
App Service authentication can use an Entra tenant to limit website access to accounts from that directory.
Deployment slots can use separate authentication settings.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: configure authentication provider aad

lessons.title: Compare Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2 plans
points: Entra ID premium editions add capabilities beyond the free directory features and require the relevant licenses.
P1 capabilities described here include Conditional Access, password reset with writeback, self-service group management and Connect Health.
P2 adds Identity Protection for risk-based account and sign-in protection.
P2 also adds Privileged Identity Management to control permanent and temporary privileged access through activation workflows.
Check current Microsoft licensing documentation before deciding which edition is required; plans and feature entitlements change.

lessons.title: Examine Microsoft Entra Domain Services
points: Entra Domain Services provides managed domain capabilities for workloads needing domain join, Group Policy or traditional authentication.
It can support applications using LDAP, NTLM or Kerberos without you operating the domain controllers.
An alternative is to connect to on-premises domain controllers over a VPN or run AD DS domain controllers on Azure virtual machines.
With on-premises directory integration, users can use organizational identities across local and cloud environments.
The managed service reduces domain-controller maintenance and replication administration, but has service-specific limitations and usage charges.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Entra ID serves cloud identity needs, AD DS provides traditional domain services, and managed Entra Domain Services supports suitable legacy application requirements.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Manage user identities, groups, licensing and device registration centrally, giving people only the access needed for their work.

lessons.title: Create, configure, and manage users
points: Manage user objects under Identity, Users, All users in the Entra admin center; switch directory before changing another tenant.
Cloud identities are managed in Entra ID; directory-synchronized identities originate in on-premises Active Directory.
Guest accounts represent people outside the organization, such as contractors, and their access should be removed when no longer needed.
Cloud Sync uses lightweight agents with cloud-managed synchronization; choose Cloud Sync or Connect Sync after comparing the capabilities your deployment requires.
User type and source help distinguish tenant members, invited guests and synchronized accounts.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: what is cloud sync

lessons.title: Exercise - assign licenses to users
points: Use a tenant where you have the required user-administration permissions to create a test user.
Create an assigned security group and add the test user as a member, with an administrator as its owner.
In the Microsoft 365 admin center, open Billing, Licenses, select a product, choose Groups and assign the license to the group.
Verify the group assignment and the resulting license on the test user.

lessons.title: Exercise - restore or remove deleted users
points: Select a test account in Entra Users and delete it, then open Deleted users to find the suspended account.
Deleted user accounts can be restored during the 30-day retention window.
Choose Restore user, confirm the operation, and verify that the account appears again under All users.
Permanent deletion cannot be undone; use the official lab instructions and required administrator role.

lessons.title: Create, configure, and manage groups
points: Use security groups to manage access to shared resources; members can include users, devices and service principals.
Use Microsoft 365 groups for collaboration resources such as shared mailboxes, calendars, files and SharePoint sites.
Assigned membership is maintained manually. Dynamic membership adds or removes members according to attribute-based rules.
Dynamic user membership works with security and Microsoft 365 groups; dynamic device membership applies only to security groups.
A change such as a user moving department can change their dynamic group memberships automatically.
Dynamic user groups require enough Entra ID P1 or Intune for Education licenses for every unique user member; dynamic device group members need no license.

lessons.title: Exercise - add groups in Microsoft Entra ID
points: In Entra Identity, Groups, create a Microsoft 365 group with Assigned membership.
Choose an owner and members, then verify the new group in All groups after refreshing if necessary.
Follow the official exercise in a tenant where you have the required user-administration permissions.

lessons.title: Configure and manage device registration
points: Entra registered devices support personal-device and mobile scenarios; users can keep local device sign-in while adding a work account.
Entra joined devices use an organizational account for device sign-in and suit cloud-first management.
Hybrid Entra joined devices remain joined to on-premises AD DS and also have an Entra device identity.
Use hybrid join when existing applications require AD machine authentication or devices must retain Group Policy and existing imaging processes.
Device identity can support Conditional Access; Intune or another management tool applies compliance and security settings.
Entra join supports Windows 10 and Windows 11 except Home editions; check current support before choosing other operating systems.
Windows Hello for Business cloud Kerberos trust enables on-premises authentication from Entra joined or hybrid joined devices after Microsoft Entra Kerberos and the required policies are configured.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: how to connect device writeback
Microsoft Learn: hybrid cloud kerberos trust

lessons.title: Manage licenses
points: Assign user service licenses through the Microsoft 365 admin center or supported administration APIs and tools.
Group-based licensing assigns product licenses to members automatically and removes inherited licenses when members leave.
Provide enough licenses for each unique member who needs the licensed product and meet the group-based licensing entitlement requirements.
A product license can have selected service plans disabled when a service is not required.
The same product assigned through multiple groups or both directly and through a group consumes one license for that user.
Set each user’s correct usage location before assignment because some services are not available in every location.
Investigate assignment errors such as insufficient licenses or conflicting services rather than assuming every group member was licensed successfully.

lessons.title: Exercise - change group license assignments
points: Review the group’s current license assignments, then change them under Billing, Licenses in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
Check processing results and user error states after the assignment; group licensing runs in the background.
Resolve insufficient licenses, conflicting service plans, missing prerequisites, unsupported usage locations or duplicate proxy addresses as applicable.
For an add-on product, assign its prerequisite service plan together with the add-on in the licensing group.
When migrating direct licenses to group assignments, first assign equivalent group licenses and verify success before removing the direct assignments.
Check a subset of users and audit logs during migration so that users do not lose services or data.
After correcting a license problem, trigger supported reprocessing where needed and verify that the user’s resulting license state is correct.

lessons.title: Exercise - change user license assignments
points: Create a test user in Entra ID and set the user’s usage location.
In Microsoft 365 Billing, Licenses, choose a product and use Assign licenses for the test account.
Verify the result on the user’s Licenses page in the Entra admin center.

lessons.title: Create custom security attributes
points: Custom security attributes are tenant-wide business-specific key-value pairs assigned to users or enterprise applications.
Use them to categorize identities and applications or support fine-grained resource-access decisions.
Attribute types are Boolean, integer and string. Integer and string attributes can allow multiple values or predefined choices; Boolean attributes are single-valued.
Attributes can also be assigned to users synchronized from on-premises AD.
The source states that custom security attributes are not supported in Entra Domain Services, SAML token claims or JWT claims.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: custom security attributes overview

lessons.title: Explore automatic user creation
points: SCIM is an open standard for exchanging identity information and automating user and group provisioning.
The Entra provisioning service connects to a target application’s SCIM endpoint using its schema and REST APIs.
An authoritative HR system can drive creation, attribute updates and deprovisioning as employees join, change roles or leave.
API-driven inbound provisioning supports sources that do not expose a SCIM endpoint by accepting workforce data from an automation tool or script.
Keep provisioning and deprovisioning connected to the identity lifecycle so that departed employees do not retain unnecessary access.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: User lifecycle, group membership, licensing and device identity work together to control access and keep organizational identities current.

modules.title: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure has a physical structure of datacenters, zones and regions, alongside a management hierarchy for resources, access and billing.

lessons.title: What is Microsoft Azure
points: Azure provides cloud services ranging from virtual machines and storage to managed databases and web applications.
Move an existing workload to virtual machines or modernize parts of it using managed services.
Scale resources up or out when demand rises and reduce them when demand falls to avoid unnecessary unused capacity.

lessons.title: Get started with Azure accounts
points: An Azure subscription is required to create and use Azure resources.
An account can have several subscriptions, allowing development, testing and production workloads to be separated.
Free and student offers have service limits and time-limited credits; check the current offer before relying on it.
When practicing in Azure, monitor usage and remove resources that are no longer needed to avoid unexpected costs.

lessons.title: Describe Azure physical infrastructure
points: A region groups nearby datacenters connected by low-latency networking. Choose a suitable region for regional resource deployments.
Service availability, virtual machine sizes and storage features differ by region; some services such as Entra ID and Azure DNS are global.
Availability zones are physically separate datacenter groups within a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking.
A zonal resource is placed in a selected zone, while a zone-redundant service replicates across zones. Not every region or service supports zones.
Region pairs can support resilience across a geography, but not every region has a traditional pair.
Do not assume regional failover or replication is automatic: individual services may require customer configuration.
Sovereign Azure environments are isolated from the main Azure environment to meet particular legal or compliance requirements.

lessons.title: Describe Azure management infrastructure
points: The management hierarchy is management group, subscription, resource group and resource.

A resource group contains resource-group-scoped resources; each belongs to one group at a time. Some resources, such as policy definitions, exist at subscription or management-group scope. Groups cannot be nested or renamed.
Deleting a resource group deletes the resources it contains, so group resources with an appropriate shared lifecycle.
A subscription is a billing and access-management boundary; separate subscriptions can isolate environments, teams or cost reporting.
Management groups organize multiple subscriptions so that governance and access settings can apply across them.
Azure RBAC assignments and Azure Policy assignments at parent scopes apply to child scopes, including subscriptions and their resources.
A tenant has a Tenant Root Group. Management groups can be nested up to six levels, excluding the root and subscription levels; each group or subscription has one parent.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Use regions and zones for physical placement and resilience, and the management hierarchy for organization, access and governance.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Policy evaluates resource configurations against governance rules and applies the configured effects.
An initiative groups policy definitions into a single assignment and compliance view for a shared governance goal.

lessons.title: Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure
points: Cloud governance is an ongoing process: build a governance team, assess risks, document policies, enforce them and monitor results.
Translate business risks and tolerance into clear rules and processes for identifying violations.
Governance policies cover regulatory compliance, security, operations, costs, data and resource management.
Azure Policy can restrict regions or VM sizes, require tags, assess existing configurations and support remediation.
Use the compliance dashboard to investigate both overall compliance and specific resource or policy results.
Balance governance controls with operational needs and test new policies before they affect important workloads.

lessons.title: Azure Policy design principles
points: Choose assignment scope carefully: management groups cover many subscriptions, while resource-group or resource scope narrows the impact.
Resource Manager handles control-plane operations such as creating and configuring resources; service data-plane operations access data directly.
Resource Manager authenticates and authorizes a control-plane request before passing it to the appropriate resource provider.
Azure Policy is integrated with Resource Manager; certain services also support specialized data-plane policy modes.
For a new or updated resource, policy evaluates the intended resource state during the request.
For existing resources, a newly assigned policy evaluates compliance through scans. A deny policy does not delete existing noncompliant resources.
Use management groups and subscriptions to organize governance rather than repeatedly configuring every resource separately.

lessons.title: Azure Policy resources
points: A definition describes the condition to test and the effect to apply; an initiative groups definitions for a shared purpose.
The definition’s location, at management-group or subscription level, limits where it can be assigned.
An assignment applies a definition or initiative at a scope and can supply parameters, exclusions, selectors and noncompliance messages.
An exemption records an accepted exception: Mitigated means the policy intent is met another way, while Waiver accepts noncompliance.
Manual policy effects use attestations to record the compliance state.
Remediation tasks can bring existing noncompliant resources into compliance for modify or deployIfNotExists assignments.
Remediation for deployIfNotExists or modify requires a managed identity on the assignment with the necessary Azure RBAC permissions.

lessons.title: Azure Policy definitions
points: A policy definition is JSON containing a policy rule and optional parameters, with metadata and mode controlling its interpretation.
The if block identifies matching resources; the then block specifies an effect.
Combine conditions with allOf, anyOf and not, and use field, value or count expressions to inspect resource properties or arrays.
Deny blocks a noncompliant resource request; audit reports a warning without blocking it.
Modify changes supported properties or tags; deployIfNotExists can deploy a related resource when its conditions are met.
AuditIfNotExists checks a related resource, denyAction can block supported deletion actions, and manual allows compliance attestation.
Disabled turns off evaluation for the assignment’s effect. When policies are layered, each is evaluated independently and the combined restrictions apply.

lessons.title: Evaluation of resources through Azure Policy
points: Policy evaluations are triggered by assignments or updates, resource changes, exemptions, subscription changes and scheduled or on-demand scans.
The standard full compliance evaluation runs every 24 hours; use az policy state trigger-scan for an on-demand evaluation when appropriate.
Compliance evaluation can take time depending on scope, policy complexity and system load; do not assume results update immediately.
Investigate noncompliant, conflicting or error states rather than relying only on the overall compliance percentage.
Set assignment enforcementMode to DoNotEnforce to evaluate compliance without enforcing policy effects; this differs from the disabled effect, which prevents evaluation.
Start new deny or modify policies without enforcement, check compliance and application health, then enable them through progressively larger deployment rings.
Azure Policy state-change events can be routed through Event Grid to handlers such as Functions, Logic Apps or a webhook.

lessons.title: Check your knowledge
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Design policy scope and effects carefully, evaluate before enforcing, and expand deployment only after compliance and application-health checks.

modules.title: Secure your Azure resources with Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure role-based access control specifies who can access Azure resources, which operations they can perform and where that access applies.

lessons.title: What is Azure RBAC?
points: A role assignment combines a security principal, a role definition and a scope: who, what and where.
Principals include users, groups and applications. A role definition lists permitted operations.
Scopes include management group, subscription, resource group and individual resource; child scopes inherit parent assignments.
Owner manages resources and access. Contributor manages resources but cannot grant access. Reader views resources. User Access Administrator manages access.
Assign the least privilege needed, using a narrow scope and a suitable built-in or custom role.
Azure RBAC permissions are additive across assignments. NotActions subtract operations from one role’s Actions but do not prevent another role from granting them.
Use Access control, also called IAM, to inspect assignments, grant access or remove role assignments.

lessons.title: Knowledge check - What is Azure RBAC?
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Exercise - List access using Azure RBAC and the Azure portal
points: Use My permissions in the Azure portal to review your own role assignments and their scopes.
Open a resource group’s Access control, IAM, and Role assignments tab to see who has access.
Distinguish assignments made at the current scope from permissions inherited from a parent scope.
Use the Roles tab to inspect built-in and custom role definitions and their assignments.

lessons.title: Exercise - Grant access using Azure RBAC and the Azure portal
points: Use an account with role-assignment permissions, such as Owner or User Access Administrator at the intended scope.
Open the resource group’s Access control, IAM, and choose Add role assignment.
Select Virtual Machine Contributor, select the intended user, then review the role, member and scope before assigning.
The assignment lets the user manage virtual machines within that resource group; its scope does not cover unrelated groups.
Remove the specific role assignment to revoke that grant, and check whether other assignments still provide access.

lessons.title: Exercise - View activity logs for Azure RBAC changes
points: Open Azure Activity Log and choose the timespan for the access-change investigation.
Filter operations for role-assignment creation or deletion and custom-role definition creation, updates or deletion.
Open an event to review its details and identify the change.
Download the filtered activity log as CSV when a report is needed.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Grant access by combining the right principal, role and scope, and use the Activity Log to investigate access changes.

modules.title: Allow users to reset their password with Microsoft Entra self-service password reset

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Self-service password reset lets eligible users recover access without waiting for an administrator to reset their password.

lessons.title: What is self-service password reset in Microsoft Entra ID?
points: Changing a known password while signed in differs from resetting a forgotten or expired password through SSPR.
The reset process identifies the user, verifies identity using configured methods, accepts a new password and can send configured notifications.
Require users to register the minimum number of permitted authentication methods before they rely on SSPR.
Administrator accounts have stronger reset requirements: two authentication methods and no security questions.
Enable user notifications to reveal unexpected resets, and enable administrator notifications so Global Administrators are alerted when another administrator resets a password.

Cloud-only password reset requires an eligible Microsoft 365 or Entra premium license. On-premises password writeback requires Entra ID P1/P2 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium plus supported synchronization configuration.
For synchronized users, password writeback sends cloud password changes back to the on-premises directory through a supported Connect or Cloud Sync deployment.

lessons.title: Implement Microsoft Entra self-service password reset
points: For the pilot described here, prepare an eligible licensed tenant, an Authentication Policy Administrator, a non-administrator test user and a security group.
Choose None to disable user SSPR, Selected to pilot with a security group, or All for tenant-wide user rollout.
Set the required number of methods in Password reset. Manage allowed methods in the Authentication methods policy; security questions remain in the SSPR policy.
Require registration at sign-in if appropriate and decide how often users should reconfirm their authentication information.
Configure user and administrator reset notifications and a custom helpdesk email address or URL.
Test with a non-administrator account because administrator reset requirements differ from ordinary users.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: concept authentication methods manage
Microsoft Learn: how to authentication methods manage

lessons.title: Exercise - Set up self-service password reset
points: Create an assigned security group for pilot users and add a non-administrator test account.
Set password reset to Selected, choose the pilot group and save the configuration.
Review the required method count, registration and notifications in Password reset, enable Email OTP for the pilot users in the Authentication methods policy, and configure the helpdesk contact.
Sign in as the test user at the official registration portal and register the email method used by this exercise.
Use the official reset portal to verify identity, receive the verification code, set a new password and confirm the reset works.
Use a separate private browser session if an existing administrator session interferes with the test.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: concept authentication methods manage
Microsoft Learn: how to authentication methods manage

lessons.title: Exercise - Customize directory branding
points: Use an eligible licensed tenant and an Organizational Branding Administrator, then prepare background and logo files to the current branding image requirements.
In the intended Entra tenant, open Company branding and configure the favicon, background image and background color.
Review and save the branding, then sign in as the test user in a new browser window to check the result.
Verify that branding also appears when the user selects the forgotten-password flow.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: how to customize branding

lessons.title: Summary
points: After a lab, remove its test user and group and turn off the pilot SSPR setting if it is no longer needed.
Keep production password-reset settings separate from temporary exercise configuration.

paths.title: AZ-104: Configure and manage virtual networks for Azure administrators

lessons.title: Introduction
points: A virtual network gives Azure resources a private network and can connect them to on-premises networks.

lessons.title: Plan virtual networks
points: Plan a virtual network as a logically isolated network with its own CIDR address space.
Choose nonoverlapping address ranges before connecting Azure networks to each other or to on-premises networks.
Control DNS settings and divide the address space into subnets suited to your workloads.
Use a cloud-only network when no on-premises connection is needed; use a site-to-site IPsec VPN for a secure hybrid connection.

lessons.title: Create subnets
points: Each subnet must use a unique, nonoverlapping CIDR range contained within the virtual network address space.
In each IPv4 subnet, Azure reserves the first four addresses and the final address; allow for these when sizing the subnet.
Leave address space for services that need dedicated subnets, such as VPN Gateway.
Azure routes between subnets by default; use custom routes when traffic must pass through a network virtual appliance.
A subnet can have at most one network security group. Its rules filter traffic to and from subnet resources.
Private Link provides private connectivity to supported services without exposing the connection to the public internet.

lessons.title: Create virtual networks
points: Create a virtual network with a subscription, resource group, name, region and planned IP address space.
Define at least one subnet inside that address space and avoid overlap with other subnet ranges.
Check current networking resource limits in Microsoft documentation before deploying a large design.

lessons.title: Plan IP addressing
points: Private IP addresses support communication inside a virtual network and over private hybrid connections such as VPN or ExpressRoute.
Public IP addresses support internet-facing communication.
Choose a static address when DNS records, firewall rules, IP-based security or server roles require a predictable address.
Use dynamic private-IP assignment when the resource does not require a fixed address; Standard public IPs use static allocation.

lessons.title: Create public IP addressing
points: For new public IPs, select a supported Standard SKU, IP version and tier; Standard public IP allocation is static. Basic public IPs retired on 30 September 2025.
The public IP SKU and tier must match the load balancer that uses it.
A static public IP is allocated when its resource is created and released when that resource is deleted.

lessons.title: Associate public IP addresses
points: Associate a VM public IP through its network interface configuration.
Load Balancer, Application Gateway and Azure Firewall use public IPs in their front-end configurations; gateways use gateway IP configurations.
Standard public IP addresses use static allocation and a secure-by-default model, with zonal and zone-redundant options where supported.

lessons.title: Allocate or assign private IP addresses
points: A private IP comes from the subnet in which the resource is deployed.
Dynamic assignment is the default: Azure selects an available address that is neither assigned nor reserved.
Static assignment lets you select an unused, unreserved address in the subnet range.
VMs use NIC IP configurations; internal load balancers and application gateways use front-end configurations.

lessons.title: Exercise: Create and configure virtual networks
points: Plan an application virtual network with separate front-end and back-end subnets, plus a hub network with a firewall subnet.
Create both networks in the same region and configure private peering between them.
The official hands-on exercise needs an Azure subscription; read its steps before choosing to deploy resources.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Size nonoverlapping networks and subnets, then choose private or public addressing for each resource.
Use segmentation and connectivity controls together to support secure communication.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Network security groups filter inbound and outbound traffic using allow and deny rules.

lessons.title: Implement network security groups
points: Associate an NSG with a subnet or a network interface to filter traffic at that scope.
One NSG can be reused across multiple associations, but each subnet or NIC can have at most one NSG.
Subnet rules affect the resources in that subnet; NIC rules affect traffic through that interface.
Inspect a VM overview to find its associated NSGs, subnets, interfaces and rules.

lessons.title: Determine network security group rules
points: An NSG includes default inbound and outbound rules. You cannot delete them, but a higher-priority custom rule can override their effect.
Define source, destination, port ranges, protocol and an allow or deny action.
Custom priorities range from 100 to 4096. A lower number is evaluated first.
Default inbound rules permit VirtualNetwork service-tag traffic and AzureLoadBalancer health probes, then deny other inbound traffic.
Default outbound rules permit virtual-network and internet traffic, then deny other outbound traffic.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Determine network security group effective rules
points: Inbound traffic is evaluated at the subnet NSG before the NIC NSG; outbound traffic is evaluated at the NIC before the subnet.
If both scopes have NSGs, traffic must be permitted by both. An allow rule at one scope cannot cancel a deny at the other.
Subnet NSGs can also affect communication between VMs in the same subnet.
Leave gaps between priority numbers so later rules can be inserted without renumbering existing rules.
Use Effective security rules to inspect the rules applying to a NIC. Network Watcher IP flow verify can identify the rule allowing or denying a proposed flow.

lessons.title: Create network security group rules
points: Create inbound or outbound rules with the required source, destination, protocol, ports, action and priority.
Predefined services such as HTTPS, SSH or RDP help populate protocol and destination-port settings.
Augmented rules can combine multiple IP ranges and port ranges to reduce separate rule definitions.
Assign lower priority numbers to rules that must be evaluated before broader rules.

lessons.title: Implement application security groups
points: An application security group groups VM network interfaces by application role, such as web servers or database servers.
Use an ASG as a source or destination in NSG rules instead of maintaining a list of individual VM IP addresses.
Assign each server NIC to the appropriate ASG, then define traffic allowed between application tiers.
For example, allow web traffic to the web tier, allow database traffic from that tier to the application tier, and explicitly deny other database sources before the default VirtualNetwork allow rule.
ASGs group your VMs; service tags represent Microsoft-managed IP prefixes for Azure services.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: network security groups overview

lessons.title: Exercise - Implement virtual networking
points: Create virtual networks and subnets, then configure ASGs and NSGs to allow required communication and deny unwanted access.
Test the resulting VM connectivity rather than relying only on the rule definitions.
The official exercise requires an Azure subscription and includes optional public and private DNS configuration.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Evaluate rule priority and both subnet and NIC scopes when troubleshooting traffic.
Use application security groups to express workload relationships without maintaining individual IP lists.

modules.title: Host your domain on Azure DNS

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure DNS hosts domain records using Azure infrastructure; domain registration remains with a registrar.

lessons.title: What is Azure DNS?
points: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses using authoritative records and cached lookup results.
Azure DNS hosts and manages zones with Azure credentials, tools, RBAC, activity logs and resource locks; it does not register domain names.
A records map names to IPv4 addresses, CNAME records map names to other names, MX records identify mail servers, and TXT records carry text such as ownership verification.
A record set groups records with the same name and type. SOA and CNAME record sets each contain only one record.
Azure creates NS and SOA records when you create a DNS zone.
Private DNS zones provide name resolution for linked virtual networks without publishing those records to the internet.
Alias record sets can reference supported Azure resources and use A, AAAA or CNAME record types.

lessons.title: Configure Azure DNS to host your domain
points: Create a public DNS zone using the registered domain name, subscription and resource group.
Retrieve its Azure DNS name servers and update domain delegation at the registrar to use all four.
Verify delegation by querying the domain SOA record with a tool such as nslookup. Allow time for DNS changes to propagate.
Create host records with the appropriate type, target and TTL; TTL determines how long a resolver may cache the record.
For private names, create a private DNS zone and add a virtual network link for each network that needs to resolve its records.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create a DNS zone and an A record by using Azure DNS
points: Create a public DNS zone, inspect its automatically created NS and SOA records, then add a www A record pointing to the example IP address.
Query the assigned Azure DNS name server to verify the A record even if the example domain has not been registered or delegated.
This exercise is optional and requires your own Azure subscription if you deploy it.

lessons.title: Dynamically resolve resource name by using alias record
points: The zone apex is the root domain, often represented by the at sign in DNS records. A conventional CNAME cannot be placed there.
Use an Azure alias record to connect a supported A or AAAA record at the apex to an Azure resource rather than hard-coding its IP address.
Supported targets include public IP resources and supported Traffic Manager, CDN and Front Door resources.
Alias records track the target resource lifecycle and changes, reducing stale or dangling references.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create alias records for Azure DNS
points: The official setup creates two VMs and a load balancer, then connects them to a public IP resource.
Create an apex A record, enable Alias record set, choose Azure resource and select the load balancer public IP resource.
Verify the test site responds through the load balancer. Registered-domain resolution also requires correct DNS delegation.
Read the optional exercise before deploying; it creates resources in your own Azure subscription.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Delegate a registered domain to Azure DNS, then use suitable record sets and aliases to resolve its services.
Remove resources created by the optional exercises when finished to avoid continuing charges.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Virtual network peering provides private communication between Azure networks in the same or different regions.

lessons.title: Determine Azure Virtual Network peering uses
points: Regional peering connects networks in the same region; global peering connects networks in different regions.
Traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone rather than traversing the public internet. Peering does not require a VPN gateway for direct network-to-network communication.
Peered virtual networks remain separately managed resources and may belong to different subscriptions or tenants.
Peered address spaces must not overlap.
Azure-provided name resolution does not automatically span peered networks; use linked private DNS zones or custom DNS for cross-network names.
Check cloud-specific and resource-specific peering support before designing connections across regions.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual network peering overview

lessons.title: Determine gateway transit and connectivity
points: Gateway transit lets a peered network use a VPN gateway in another network, commonly a hub.
Configure the hub to allow gateway transit and the spoke to use the remote gateway. A spoke using a remote gateway cannot also have its own gateway.
Peering settings also control traffic to the remote network and acceptance of traffic forwarded from that network.
A virtual network can have only one VPN gateway; gateway transit avoids deploying a separate gateway in each spoke.
Gateway transit supports regional and global peering and can extend connectivity to site-to-site, point-to-site or other network connections.
NSG rules still control which traffic is permitted between the networks.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual network peering overview

lessons.title: Create virtual network peering
points: Prepare two virtual networks and an account with Network Contributor or equivalent peering permissions.
Create the peering relationships and select the required traffic and gateway settings in the portal, CLI or PowerShell.
Verify that the peering status is Connected on both networks. An Initiated status on only one side is not a completed connection.

lessons.title: Extend peering with user-defined routes and service chaining
points: Peering is not transitive: peering A to B and B to C does not automatically connect A to C.
A hub-and-spoke design centralizes shared NVAs or gateways in the hub.
Use user-defined routes to send traffic to an NVA or VPN gateway in a peered network for service chaining; an ExpressRoute gateway cannot be a UDR next hop.
Azure Virtual Network Manager can centrally manage hub-and-spoke or mesh connectivity at scale.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual networks udr overview
Microsoft Learn: virtual network peering overview

lessons.title: Exercise - Implement Intersite Connectivity
points: Deploy test VMs into separate networks and verify the initial connectivity using Network Watcher or PowerShell.
Configure network peerings, then test connectivity again; the exercise also offers an optional custom route.
The official hands-on lab requires your own Azure subscription.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Use private peering for direct connectivity and gateway transit for shared access to external networks.
Extend nontransitive peering designs with explicit routing and service chaining when required.

modules.title: Manage and control traffic flow in your Azure deployment with routes

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Custom routes control traffic paths, including sending traffic through a network virtual appliance for inspection.

lessons.title: Identify routing capabilities of an Azure virtual network
points: Azure installs system routes for each subnet. You cannot delete these routes, but user-defined routes can override applicable defaults.
A route combines a destination address prefix with a next hop such as virtual network, internet, virtual appliance, VPN gateway or None; None drops matching traffic.
Use a route table and user-defined routes to direct traffic through a firewall or other network virtual appliance.
Service tags let Microsoft maintain the address prefixes for a supported Azure service instead of you tracking IP changes manually.
BGP exchanges routes between Azure gateways and on-premises networks over supported VPN or ExpressRoute connections.

Azure normally chooses the longest matching prefix, then prefers UDR, BGP and system routes for equal prefixes. Preferred system routes for VNets, peering and service endpoints override BGP; service-endpoint routes cannot be overridden by UDRs.
Do not create multiple user-defined routes with the same address prefix in one route table.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual networks udr overview

lessons.title: Exercise - Create custom routes
points: Create a route table and add a route for the private subnet with next-hop type Virtual appliance and the appliance private IP.
Create public, private and perimeter subnets, then associate the route table with the public subnet.
The example directs public-to-private traffic through an appliance that will be deployed in the perimeter subnet. The optional exercise requires an Azure subscription.

lessons.title: What is an NVA?
points: An NVA is a VM-based network function such as a firewall, router, proxy or intrusion detection appliance.
Place it in the traffic path with user-defined routes and enable IP forwarding on its network interface and inside its operating system.
Separate workloads into subnets when the appliance must inspect traffic flowing between them.
Each subnet can use one route table; a route table can be associated with multiple subnets.
An appliance in the traffic path becomes a dependency for connectivity, so design high availability rather than relying on a single failing instance.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create an NVA and virtual machines
points: Deploy the example Ubuntu VM into the perimeter subnet to act as the network appliance.
Enable IP forwarding on the Azure NIC and in the guest operating system; both are needed for forwarded traffic to reach its destination.
Use the official optional instructions for the exact commands; deployment uses your own Azure subscription.

lessons.title: Exercise - Route traffic through the NVA
points: Deploy public and private test VMs with traceroute available, then wait for deployment and package installation to complete.
Trace the public-to-private path: the first hop should be the NVA and the next hop the private VM.
Trace the return direction separately. In this example, the private subnet uses system routes and reaches the public VM directly.
This shows that a route table affects the associated source subnet; configuring one direction does not automatically configure the reverse path.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Use route tables and correctly configured forwarding to send subnet traffic through an NVA.
Delete optional lab resources when finished so charges do not continue.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Load Balancer distributes network traffic across VMs or scale-set instances using rules and health probes.

lessons.title: What is Azure Load Balancer?
points: Use a public load balancer for internet-facing traffic and an internal load balancer for a private front end.
The public front end maps incoming IP and port combinations to private back-end addresses and ports.
Internal load balancing supports private application tiers and on-premises access over suitable hybrid connections.
Rules determine distribution; health probes prevent new traffic being directed to unhealthy back-end instances.

lessons.title: How Azure Load Balancer works
points: Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and makes decisions using IP addresses, TCP or UDP and ports, rather than HTTP host names or URL paths.
Configure a front-end IP, a back-end pool, load-balancing rules and health probes. A rule maps a front-end IP and port to back-end IPs and ports.
The default distribution hashes source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol. Client IP affinity uses fewer fields to keep related connections on a back-end instance.
TCP probes check connection establishment; HTTP and HTTPS probes expect a successful HTTP 200 response. A failed probe stops new connections to the affected instance.
Inbound NAT rules map front-end ports to individual back-end instances, for example for administration.
HA port rules on an internal Standard load balancer balance TCP and UDP flows across all ports, useful for highly available NVAs.
Outbound rules configure SNAT for back-end instances that need access to public endpoints.

lessons.title: When to use Azure Load Balancer
points: Choose Load Balancer for high-performance TCP or UDP traffic and private or public VM application tiers.
Use Application Gateway when routing must inspect HTTP host names or URL paths, or needs regional web application firewall features.
Use Front Door for global Layer 7 delivery and acceleration across regions; Traffic Manager distributes traffic using DNS.
A single lightly used server may not need load balancing; choose the service from application and availability requirements.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Load Balancer combines Layer 4 rules, health probes and optional affinity to distribute traffic reliably.
Distinguish it from Layer 7 Application Gateway and Front Door, and DNS-based Traffic Manager.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Application Gateway manages web requests with load balancing, TLS processing and optional web application firewall protection.

lessons.title: What is Azure Application Gateway?
points: Application Gateway routes HTTP traffic to pools containing VMs, scale sets, App Service apps or reachable on-premises servers.
It balances requests across healthy back ends; session stickiness can keep a client session on the same server.
It supports TLS termination and end-to-end encryption, plus optional WAF protection against common web attacks.
Standard_v2 and WAF_v2 support autoscaling as traffic changes; connection draining supports graceful removal of back-end servers.

lessons.title: How Azure Application Gateway works
points: A front-end IP receives traffic. A listener matches a protocol, port, host and IP combination, and a routing rule connects that listener to a back-end pool.
Layer 7 path-based routing sends different URL paths to different pools; multi-site listeners route using host names.
Back-end HTTP settings define protocol, timeout, session affinity, connection draining and probe behavior.
TLS termination decrypts incoming traffic at the gateway to offload back-end work. Configure HTTPS to the back end when traffic must be re-encrypted.
Optional WAF policies inspect requests for threats such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting before requests reach the application.
Health probes determine eligible back ends; HTTP responses from 200 through 399 are normally healthy for the probe described here.

Additional features include redirects, header rewrites, custom error pages, v2 autoscaling and WebSocket support. HTTP/2 is supported on client-to-gateway connections; back-end HTTP connections use HTTP/1.1.

lessons.title: When to use Azure Application Gateway
points: Choose Application Gateway for regional HTTP routing, TLS offload, session affinity and optional WAF protection.
It can front reachable on-premises web servers as well as Azure-hosted web applications.
Choose Front Door for global web delivery, Traffic Manager for DNS-based distribution, or Load Balancer for Layer 4 TCP and UDP traffic.
Decide whether the application actually needs a pool and gateway before adding this service.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Use listeners, routing rules, back-end settings and health probes together to route web requests.
Add TLS and optional WAF controls according to the security requirements of the application.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Network Watcher provides monitoring and diagnostic tools for networking used by Azure IaaS resources.

lessons.title: What is Azure Network Watcher?
points: Use Topology to see resource relationships and Connection Monitor to track connectivity and latency over time.
IP flow verify identifies whether traffic is allowed or denied and which security rule applies. NSG diagnostics examines filtering for supported resources.
Next hop reports the route, next-hop type and IP used for a destination; Effective security rules combines applicable subnet and NIC rules.
Connection troubleshoot tests connectivity at a point in time rather than continuously monitoring it.
Packet capture records traffic for detailed analysis; VPN troubleshoot diagnoses virtual network gateways and their connections.
Virtual network flow logs record IP traffic in storage, and Traffic analytics visualizes it. New NSG flow logs cannot be created; existing NSG flow logs retire on 30 September 2027.
Network Watcher is primarily for IaaS networking, rather than general PaaS monitoring or website analytics.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: nsg flow logs overview

lessons.title: How Azure Network Watcher works
points: Creating or updating a virtual network normally enables Network Watcher in that subscription and region. If automatic enablement was previously disabled, enable it manually; open the tool through portal search.
Topology shows resources and their Contains or Associated relationships so you can inspect the network layout.
Connection Monitor probes endpoints at intervals. Azure VM sources need the Network Watcher extension; on-premises sources need Azure Arc and Azure Monitor Agent.
For IP flow verify, provide the VM, NIC, local and remote IPs and ports, protocol and direction.
Next hop uses effective NIC routes to identify whether packets go to the intended network, gateway or appliance.
Packet capture uses the VM extension, accepts traffic filters and saves captured data to disk or blob storage.
Connection troubleshooting can identify DNS, guest firewall, NSG, route, CPU or memory issues; VPN diagnostics return health details and recommended actions.

lessons.title: When to use Azure Network Watcher
points: Use IP flow verify to investigate an NSG blocking communication, such as a required management port between VMs.
Use VPN troubleshoot for gateway and site-to-site connection health, then inspect its diagnostic logs and recommendations.
Measure endpoint latency across regions or hybrid connections before changing workload placement.
For PaaS service issues or website analytics, use the appropriate service-specific monitoring and health tools instead.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Choose the Network Watcher tool that matches the problem: filtering, routing, continuous connectivity, packet details or VPN health.

paths.title: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage in Azure

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Choose storage services, performance and redundancy to fit your data and recovery requirements.

lessons.title: Implement Azure Storage
points: Azure Storage provides managed services for objects, file shares, messages and nonrelational structured data.
Use managed disks for VM block storage, Blob Storage for unstructured objects and suitable data services for application records.
Redundancy protects against hardware or wider failures; encryption and access controls protect data access.
Access services through supported APIs, SDKs, CLI, PowerShell, the portal or Storage Explorer.
Blob SFTP requires hierarchical namespace. Blob NFSv3 also requires hierarchical namespace and lets Linux clients mount containers.
The portal can default to Microsoft Entra authorization instead of Shared Key authorization.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: secure file transfer protocol support
Microsoft Learn: network file system protocol support

lessons.title: Explore Azure Storage services
points: Blob Storage stores large volumes of unstructured objects such as images, media, backups and archived data.
Azure Files provides managed file shares using SMB or NFS for applications that expect shared files.
Queue Storage holds messages for asynchronous processing, decoupling work such as image uploads from thumbnail generation.
A queue message can be up to 64 KB; queues can hold large backlogs of messages.
Table Storage is a schemaless key-and-attribute store for structured, nonrelational data.
Choose the service by the access pattern and data model rather than treating objects, file shares, queues and tables as interchangeable.

lessons.title: Determine storage account types
points: Standard general-purpose v2 supports blobs, Data Lake Storage, queues, tables and Azure Files, and is suitable for most general storage scenarios.
Premium block blob accounts target high transaction rates and consistent low object-storage latency.
Premium FileStorage accounts provide high-performance file shares; premium page blob accounts provide page blobs for suitable I/O-intensive workloads.
Account types have different service and redundancy support: premium options are more specialized than general-purpose v2.
You cannot directly convert a Standard account into Premium or the reverse; create the desired type and move applicable data.
Legacy general-purpose v1 and BlobStorage accounts can be upgraded to general-purpose v2 to gain current capabilities.

lessons.title: Determine replication strategies
points: LRS keeps replicas within one datacenter and has the lowest cost, but a datacenter-wide disaster can affect every replica.
ZRS synchronously copies data across three availability zones in one region, maintaining access through a zone failure where supported.
GRS keeps local replicas in the primary region and asynchronously copies them to a secondary region. The secondary is not normally a read endpoint before failover.
RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary region without waiting for failover.
GZRS combines zone replication in the primary region with geographic replication to a secondary region; RA-GZRS adds secondary read access.
Compare the failure scope you must survive, required secondary access, region availability and supported account type before choosing redundancy.
Asynchronous cross-region replication means the secondary copy may lag the primary.

lessons.title: Access storage
points: A storage account has separate service endpoints such as account-name.blob.core.windows.net and account-name.file.core.windows.net.
A blob URL adds the container and blob path to the Blob service endpoint.
Map a custom subdomain to a blob or static-website endpoint with a DNS CNAME. Direct mapping supports HTTP; use Azure Front Door or a supported CDN configuration for HTTPS on the custom domain.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: storage custom domain name

lessons.title: Secure storage endpoints
points: Storage firewall and virtual-network rules can restrict network access to permitted subnets or public IP ranges.
A service endpoint retains the service public endpoint while identifying permitted virtual-network traffic.

A private endpoint gives one storage service a private IP in your virtual network. Configure DNS to resolve that endpoint and separately restrict public access if private-only connectivity is required.
Test permitted and denied network paths after configuration to confirm access matches the intended restrictions.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Select the data service and account type first, then choose redundancy and secure network access for the workload.
Storage availability, performance, security and cost depend on the configuration rather than one universal account choice.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Blob Storage stores unstructured objects; access tiers and lifecycle rules help balance retrieval needs against storage cost.

lessons.title: Implement Azure Blob Storage
points: Blob Storage organizes text or binary objects inside containers within a storage account.
Use it for browser content, media streaming, distributed downloads, backup, archive and data analysis.
Plan container access, blob types, upload tools, access tiers, lifecycle rules and object replication as part of configuration.

lessons.title: Create blob containers
points: Every blob belongs to a container, so create a container before uploading its blobs.
Container names must be unique within the account, 3 to 63 characters long and use lowercase letters, numbers or hyphens. Start and end with a letter or number; consecutive hyphens are not allowed.
Private access blocks anonymous reads. Blob access allows anonymous blob reads; Container access additionally allows anonymous listing.
Anonymous container settings only work when account-level anonymous blob access is enabled. Keep it disabled unless you need public content.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: naming and referencing containers  blobs  and metadata

lessons.title: Assign blob access tiers
points: Hot storage suits frequent access: storage costs are higher and access costs lower than cooler tiers.
Cool suits infrequent access and Cold less frequent access; both remain online. In general-purpose v2 accounts, their minimum billable storage durations are 30 and 90 days respectively.
Archive is offline for block blobs that can tolerate hours of retrieval latency, with a 180-day minimum billable duration. It supports LRS, GRS and RA-GRS, not zone-redundant account configurations.
Deleting, overwriting or moving data before the tier minimum can incur prorated early-deletion charges; the duration is a billing rule, not a deletion prohibition.
Rehydrate archived blobs to an online tier by copying to a new blob or changing the tier in place. Standard and high-priority retrieval have different latency and costs.
Choose a tier using total storage, access and retrieval requirements rather than storage price alone.

lessons.title: Add blob lifecycle management rules
points: Lifecycle management policies transition eligible blobs to cooler tiers or delete them when conditions are met.
Rules can apply to current versions, previous versions or snapshots, depending on the selected action.
Filter the affected data by container, name prefix or blob index tags rather than always acting on the entire account.
Configure an age or access-related condition and the resulting tier change or deletion action in an if-then rule.
Account and blob types determine which lifecycle features are supported; general-purpose v2 is recommended for new general-purpose deployments.
Consider minimum storage durations and retrieval needs before automatically moving data to colder storage.

lessons.title: Determine blob object replication
points: Object replication asynchronously copies selected block blobs between source and destination containers. It supports general-purpose v2 or premium block blob accounts without hierarchical namespace.
The replicated data includes blob content, metadata and versions; blob snapshots are not replicated.
Enable blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source account before configuring replication.
Policies identify source and destination accounts and contain rules selecting containers and blobs.
Source and destination blobs can use different online tiers. Moving either blob to Archive causes replication to fail; use replication for nearby reads or regional compute workloads.

lessons.title: Manage blobs
points: Block blobs are the usual choice for files, images and other text or binary objects.
Append blobs optimize adding blocks and fit logging workloads; page blobs suit frequent indexed or random read-write operations.
A blob type cannot be changed after creation.
Use the portal for a few uploads, selecting blob type, access tier and encryption options as needed.
Use Storage Explorer for graphical management, AzCopy for command-line transfers, or Data Box Disk when a large offline transfer is more practical than uploading over the network.

lessons.title: Determine Blob Storage pricing
points: Estimate costs with the Azure pricing calculator using data volume, operations, redundancy and transfer needs.
Cooler tiers reduce capacity cost but increase access and retrieval charges.
Transactions, outbound bandwidth and geo-replication transfers can contribute to the bill.
Tier changes can incur operation or data-access charges, so include migration and expected access patterns in the estimate.

lessons.title: Exercise - Provide storage for the public website
points: Create a highly available storage account and a container for website documents.
For this public-content scenario, explicitly configure anonymous access and enable soft delete and blob versioning for recovery.
Use the official exercise for deployment instructions; it requires an Azure subscription.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Choose blob type, tier and lifecycle policy from how the data is used and how quickly it must be retrieved.
Use asynchronous object replication where regional data distribution is needed.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Combine identity, restricted access, transport protection and encryption to secure stored data.

lessons.title: Review Azure Storage security strategies
points: Storage service encryption encrypts data at rest with AES-256; encryption and decryption are transparent to applications.
Require secure transfer and avoid deprecated TLS versions for connections to the account.
Prefer Microsoft Entra authorization with managed identities and scoped data-access roles when supported.
Shared Key authorization uses an account key; disabling Shared Key helps enforce identity-based authorization where the workload supports it.
A shared access signature delegates limited permissions for a limited time without handing the client the account key.
Keep anonymous access disabled for sensitive data and use logs to investigate access and usage.

lessons.title: Create shared access signatures
points: A SAS delegates access to selected storage resources with defined permissions and validity times.

A user delegation SAS is signed with a key obtained using Microsoft Entra credentials. Current support includes Blob Storage, Data Lake Storage, queues, tables and Azure Files; service and account SAS are signed with an account key.
Stored access policies add server-side control for supported service SAS, including changing or revoking access without replacing an account key.
Distribute SAS URLs only over HTTPS, grant the minimum permissions and use short validity periods.
Account for clock skew: omit an immediate start time or allow an appropriate margin, and renew before expiry.
Validate data uploaded using a SAS before the application trusts or processes it.
For high-risk operations, a validating application service may provide more control than giving a client direct storage access.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: create user delegation sas

lessons.title: Identify URI and SAS parameters
points: A SAS URL consists of the storage resource URL followed by a signed query token.
The sv parameter identifies the storage service version; st and se specify start and expiry times in UTC.
The sp parameter lists permissions, and applicable resource or service parameters identify the permitted scope.
The sip parameter can restrict caller IP addresses; spr can restrict requests to HTTPS.
The sig parameter carries the signature that authenticates the token. Treat the complete SAS URL as a credential and avoid exposing it.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: create user delegation sas

lessons.title: Determine Azure Storage encryption
points: Azure Storage automatically encrypts data before persistence and decrypts it for authorized reads; encryption at rest cannot be disabled.
Microsoft-managed keys are managed by Azure; customer-managed keys give you control over the encryption key lifecycle.
Infrastructure encryption provides a second encryption layer with a separate key and algorithm when enabled.
Account access keys authorize Shared Key requests and signed SAS tokens; they are distinct from the keys used for storage encryption.
Store access keys securely and plan rotation so applications update their credentials without losing access.

lessons.title: Create customer-managed keys
points: Customer-managed encryption keys can be stored in a customer-owned Key Vault or Managed HSM.
You can generate a new key or use an existing key, and control its access, auditing, rotation and disabling.
Select the customer-managed vault and key or enter its URI. Enable vault soft delete and purge protection, and grant the storage managed identity the required key permissions.
Choose customer-managed keys when compliance or organizational policy requires control of the encryption key lifecycle.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: customer managed keys overview

lessons.title: Apply Azure Storage security best practices
points: Storage Insights provides a consolidated view of storage performance, capacity and availability using metrics and logs.
Track latency, throughput, transaction counts and usage trends, and use alerts to investigate anomalies.
Microsoft Defender for Storage provides threat detection, including supported malware scanning and suspicious-activity detection capabilities.
Use operational monitoring and threat protection together; viewing metrics alone does not replace access controls or active threat detection.

lessons.title: Exercise: Manage Azure Storage
points: Create a storage account, secure blob containers and configure file shares using the official lab instructions.
Check how the chosen authorization and network settings protect both blob and file access.
The hands-on lab requires an Azure subscription; reading the steps does not deploy anything.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Apply least-privilege access and limited SAS credentials alongside encryption and secure transport.
Select customer-managed keys and monitoring according to your security and compliance requirements.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Files provides managed file shares, while Azure File Sync adds local Windows Server caching for hybrid access.

lessons.title: Compare storage for file shares and blob data
points: Choose Azure Files when applications expect shared directories and file-system access over SMB or NFS.
Use file shares for lift-and-shift applications, common tools, configuration files and shared diagnostic data.
Choose Blob Storage for object-oriented access to large amounts of unstructured data using REST APIs and client libraries.
Azure File Sync can centralize files in Azure while preserving local file-server access and caching.

lessons.title: Manage Azure file shares
points: Choose either SMB or NFS for a file share; a single share does not serve both protocols.
For classic shares, general-purpose v2 accounts provide HDD pay-as-you-go storage. FileStorage accounts support SSD provisioned shares and, with StandardV2 SKUs, HDD provisioned v2 shares.
HDD pay-as-you-go access tiers are Transaction optimized, Hot and Cool, with different capacity and transaction pricing. Provisioned shares use a separate billing model.
SMB identity authentication supports AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos. Configure both share-level access and Windows file/directory permissions.
Account keys provide broad access and should not be shared casually. A file SAS is for REST API access rather than mounting an SMB share.
SMB uses port 445; blocked outbound port 445 is a common cause of failed mounts from on-premises networks.

lessons.title: Create file share snapshots
points: A share snapshot is an incremental, read-only point-in-time copy of an Azure file share.
Take snapshots before risky changes or on a schedule to recover from accidental edits, deletion or application corruption.
Restore individual files, folders or a share from the appropriate snapshot.
A share can have up to 200 snapshots; they use the share redundancy settings and remain until deleted.

Deleting a share removes its snapshots too, so snapshots alone do not protect the entire share. With share soft delete enabled, undeleting the share restores its contents and snapshots during retention.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: storage files prevent file share deletion

lessons.title: Implement soft delete for Azure Files
points: Enable soft delete at the storage account level to retain deleted classic file shares temporarily; this feature does not apply to standalone Microsoft.FileShares resources.
Choose a retention period from 1 to 365 days during which a deleted share can be recovered.
Soft delete protects share deletion; use snapshots or backup for point-in-time recovery of changed or deleted files within a share.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: storage files prevent file share deletion

lessons.title: Use Azure Storage Explorer
points: Storage Explorer is a desktop tool for managing storage data across accounts and subscriptions on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Full access requires the appropriate management-plane and data-plane permissions; seeing an account does not automatically grant access to its data.
Connect through an Azure subscription, account credentials or a suitably scoped SAS, including selected services in another subscription.
An account has two access keys so clients can use one while you rotate the other; update dependent applications when credentials change.
Protect keys because they grant broad account access, and prefer appropriately scoped identity permissions where supported.

lessons.title: Consider Azure File Sync
points: Azure File Sync centralizes file shares in Azure Files while Windows Servers act as local caches.
A Storage Sync Service manages sync groups; each sync group contains one cloud endpoint and participating server endpoints.
