The cloud endpoint is an SMB Azure file share; a server endpoint identifies a local NTFS path on a registered Windows Server. Azure File Sync does not support NFS Azure file shares.
Install the Azure File Sync agent on each participating server to perform synchronization.
Cloud tiering keeps frequently accessed data local and recalls other files from Azure as needed.
Use the design for branch-office caching, hybrid application access and recovery scenarios while retaining familiar local file protocols.

lessons.title: Knowledge check
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Use file shares for native shared-file workloads and File Sync for hybrid caching.
Combine snapshots, share soft delete and appropriate backup with scoped access to protect and recover files.

paths.title: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure virtual machines provide on-demand compute with control over the guest operating system and installed software.
Plan the network, capacity, availability and backups before migrating a server.

lessons.title: Compile a checklist for creating an Azure Virtual Machine
points: Plan the virtual network, subnets and required traffic before creating the VM; connected networks must use nonoverlapping address ranges.
Azure reserves the first four and last IP addresses in each subnet. Network security groups filter traffic at subnet or network-interface level.
Inventory the operating system, CPU, memory, disk input/output and data-location requirements. Choose the region and VM size for those needs.
General-purpose sizes balance CPU and memory; compute-, memory- and storage-optimized sizes target different bottlenecks. GPU and high-performance-compute sizes serve specialized workloads.
Resizing a running VM restarts it. If a size is unavailable on its current cluster, stop and deallocate first to select another size available in the region.
Keep durable application data on data disks rather than temporary storage. VM size limits attached disks and network interfaces.
Deallocating stops compute charges, but retained disks still incur storage charges. Choose pay-as-you-go for variable use or reservations for predictable long-term use.

lessons.title: Exercise - Create a VM using the Azure portal
points: This optional exercise requires an Azure subscription and a resource group. You can study the instructions without deploying.
In the portal, create a virtual machine and choose its subscription, resource group, region, Ubuntu image and size.
Use SSH public-key authentication, supply an administrator username and generate or provide a key pair. The exercise enables SSH on port 22.
Review and validate the configuration, create the VM and securely download the private key when prompted.
After deployment, open the VM overview and use its public IP address with an SSH client.

lessons.title: Describe the options available to create and manage an Azure Virtual Machine
points: ARM templates declare resources in JSON and can parameterize names and settings for repeatable deployments. Exporting a resource template provides a starting point.
Azure CLI is cross-platform; az vm create creates a VM. Azure PowerShell provides cmdlets such as New-AzVM.
Terraform uses configuration files and a previewable execution plan to manage infrastructure.
REST APIs expose resource operations over HTTP; client SDKs wrap those APIs for application code.
VM extensions configure software after deployment. Automation can coordinate recurring management tasks.
Auto-shutdown schedules when a VM shuts down; configure the time and time zone to avoid unnecessary running time.

lessons.title: Manage the availability of your Azure VMs
points: A physical-host failure can interrupt a VM while Azure moves it to a healthy host. Platform maintenance can also require a restart.
Deploy redundant application instances across availability zones to reduce exposure to a datacenter failure. Each zone has independent power, cooling and networking.
Scale sets manage groups of VMs and can change instance counts based on demand or a schedule. They can be deployed across zones.
A load balancer distributes requests across healthy instances; redundancy still requires multiple working application instances.
Choose storage replication based on regional failure protection, cost and whether secondary-region read access is needed.
Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads to another location and coordinates failover and failback. Test recovery plans before relying on them.

lessons.title: Back up your virtual machines
points: Azure Backup protects Azure VMs and selected on-premises workloads using components appropriate to the workload.
A Recovery Services vault manages backup data, recovery points and policies. Define when backups run and how long to retain them.
Application-consistent backups capture the information needed for application recovery, rather than relying only on a disk copy.
Backup storage is managed by the service; choose redundancy, encryption and retention to meet recovery requirements.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Select VM deployment tools for repeatability, then combine availability and backup services with the recovery needs of the application.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Availability planning combines redundant VM placement with scaling rules that match changing demand.

lessons.title: Plan for maintenance and downtime
points: Plan for predicted hardware failure, unexpected host failure and scheduled platform maintenance.
Live migration can move a VM off failing hardware with a short pause; performance can still be affected.
Unexpected hardware failure can trigger a reboot on another host and loss of temporary-drive contents.
Azure maintains the physical platform; you remain responsible for updates to the guest operating system and application software.

lessons.title: Create availability sets
points: An availability set spreads related VMs across physical infrastructure to reduce shared hardware and maintenance failures.
Assign a VM to its availability set when creating the VM; changing that assignment requires recreation.
Use multiple VMs for redundancy and separate availability sets for different application tiers. Add load balancing to distribute traffic.
Availability sets do not protect against application or guest-operating-system failures; retain backup and recovery plans.

lessons.title: Review update domains and fault domains
points: An update domain groups VMs that can be restarted together during planned maintenance. Azure restarts only one update domain at a time.
Availability sets support 1 to 20 update domains, defaulting to five. The count cannot be changed after creation.
A fault domain groups VMs sharing infrastructure such as power or network switches. Distributing instances across fault domains reduces common hardware-failure exposure.
Each VM in an availability set belongs to one update domain and one fault domain.

lessons.title: Review availability zones
points: An availability zone is a separate physical location within an Azure region with independent power, cooling and networking.
Enabled regions have at least three separate zones. Distribute application instances across zones to withstand a datacenter failure.
Zonal resources are pinned to a chosen zone; zone-redundant services replicate across zones automatically.
Managed disks and VMs can be zonal, while supported storage and database offerings can provide zone redundancy.

lessons.title: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling
points: Vertical scaling changes a VM size, increasing or decreasing its CPU and memory capacity.
Horizontal scaling changes the number of VM instances serving the workload.
Vertical scaling is bounded by available hardware sizes and often requires a restart. Horizontal scaling provides more flexibility for distributing demand.
If scaling requires recreating a VM, plan how durable data is preserved and what interruption users experience.

lessons.title: Implement Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
points: Virtual Machine Scale Sets deploy and centrally manage groups of VMs and can add or remove instances manually or through autoscale.
Uniform orchestration uses a shared base image and configuration. Flexible orchestration permits differing VM configurations within a scale set.
Choose the orchestration mode when creating the scale set.
Use Azure Load Balancer for layer-four traffic distribution or Application Gateway for layer-seven routing and TLS termination.
Multiple application instances help maintain service when one instance fails.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual machine scale sets orchestration modes

lessons.title: Create Virtual Machine Scale Sets
points: When creating a scale set, choose orchestration mode, image, architecture, size and instance count.
Flexible orchestration is recommended for new deployments and supports identical or mixed VMs. Choose Uniform when its scale-set VM model and feature set fit the workload.
Check application compatibility before selecting x64 or Arm64 architecture.
Maximum spreading places instances across as many available fault domains as possible; fixed spreading can fail when its required fault domains are unavailable.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: virtual machine scale sets orchestration modes

lessons.title: Implement autoscale
points: Autoscale changes instance counts as sustained workload demand changes.
Set scale-out rules to add capacity under increased load and scale-in rules to remove unneeded capacity when demand falls.
Use schedules for predictable demand changes such as working hours or regular events.
Match thresholds to acceptable application performance rather than reacting to every brief spike.

lessons.title: Configure autoscale
points: Choose manual capacity for a fixed instance count, or autoscale for metric- or schedule-driven changes.
Set minimum, maximum and default instance counts so capacity remains within operating and cost limits.
Define scale-out and scale-in thresholds and the number of instances each action adds or removes.
Set the metric averaging period to allow readings to stabilize, and configure schedules where demand is predictable.
A scale-in policy determines which VM instances are removed.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Availability sets and zones reduce shared failures; scale sets and autoscale adjust capacity to workload demand.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: An App Service plan determines the compute capacity and scaling features available to its web apps.

lessons.title: Implement Azure App Service plans
points: An App Service plan defines the operating system, region, pricing tier, instance size and instance count.
Multiple apps can share a plan and its compute resources, potentially reducing cost.
Check remaining capacity before adding an app; overloading shared resources can affect every app in the plan.
Use a separate plan for a resource-intensive app, independent scaling or a different region.

lessons.title: Determine Azure App Service plan pricing
points: The pricing tier determines available features and how apps run and scale. Compare hardware needs with requirements such as backups and staging slots.
Free and Shared tiers use shared compute, apply CPU quotas and do not scale out; they are intended for development and testing without an SLA.
Basic, Standard and Premium tiers provide dedicated compute shared only by apps in that plan.
Isolated tiers add dedicated network isolation through App Service environments.
Apps in the same plan share instance capacity and generally scale together. Higher tiers provide additional scaling and deployment features.

lessons.title: Scale up and scale out Azure App Service
points: Scale up by changing the plan tier or instance size to obtain more CPU, memory, storage or features.
Scale out by increasing the number of instances; the selected tier limits the available count.
Rule-based autoscale adjusts instance counts according to metrics or schedules.
Plan scaling affects apps sharing the plan, but does not automatically scale dependencies such as Azure SQL or Storage.
Scale down when higher capacity or features are no longer required; confirm the lower tier still supports the app.

lessons.title: Configure Azure App Service autoscale
points: Configure autoscale profiles with minimum, maximum and safe default instance counts. When metrics are unavailable, autoscale scales out to the default only if current capacity is lower; it does not scale in to the default.
A metric rule combines a trigger with a scale-in or scale-out action. Scheduled profiles apply capacity limits and rules at specified times.
Use both scale-out and scale-in rules so performance can recover under load and unnecessary instances can be removed afterward.
Choose the appropriate metric statistic and leave adequate space between the minimum and maximum capacity.
Configure email or webhook notifications to observe scaling events.
Automatic scaling is a separate HTTP-traffic-driven feature on Premium v2, v3 and v4, configured per app with always-ready instances and no custom scaling rules.
Choose rule-based autoscale for custom metrics or schedules; consider automatic scaling for unpredictable HTTP traffic with less rule management.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Select an App Service plan for the required features and workload, then use scaling to balance capacity and cost.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure App Service hosts web apps, mobile backends and APIs without managing their underlying servers directly.

lessons.title: Implement Azure App Service
points: App Service supports web apps and APIs on Windows or Linux using supported languages and frameworks.
Deployment integrations connect source repositories and build pipelines to application releases.
Apps can scale vertically or horizontally, subject to the selected App Service plan.
Built-in authentication, IP restrictions and managed identities support application security.

lessons.title: Create an app with App Service
points: Choose a unique app name, code or container publishing, runtime stack, operating system, region and App Service plan.
The runtime stack determines the supported language and version; Linux or custom-container apps can provide a startup command.
Always On keeps an app loaded during idle periods and is required for continuous or CRON-triggered WebJobs.
Session affinity routes a client to the same instance during its session. HTTPS Only redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS.

lessons.title: Explore continuous integration and deployment
points: Configure deployment sources through Deployment Center. Continuous deployment publishes updates through a repeatable pipeline.
GitHub integration can use GitHub Actions or App Service Build Service. Other supported sources include Azure Repos and Bitbucket.
Build and release pipelines can compile code and run tests before deploying.
Manual deployment includes pushing to the app remote Git endpoint.

lessons.title: Create deployment slots
points: Deployment slots are live apps with their own hostnames, available on supported Standard, Premium and Isolated tiers.
Deploy to a staging slot to validate an update before swapping it into production.
A swap moves app content and eligible configuration between slots; the previous production version remains in the other slot for rollback.
Swapping a warmed deployment can reduce interruption compared with replacing production content directly.

lessons.title: Add deployment slots
points: Create a slot with empty content or clone configuration from an existing slot.
Some settings follow app content during a swap; slot-specific settings remain attached to the slot.
App settings, connection strings and mounted storage can be marked as slot-specific.
Custom domains, scale settings, managed identities and virtual network integration stay with their slots. Review configuration before swapping.

lessons.title: Secure your App Service app
points: App Service built-in authentication runs separately from application code and can authenticate users, handle tokens and pass identity information in headers.
You can instead use authentication supplied by your application framework.
Allow anonymous requests when the application should decide how to handle unauthenticated visitors.
Requiring authentication for every request can also restrict access to a public home page.
Use authentication logs and failed-request traces to investigate sign-in failures.

lessons.title: Create custom domain names
points: A custom domain maps a domain you control to the default App Service hostname.
Use an A record to map to an IP address or a CNAME to map to another hostname. A CNAME remains valid when the target IP changes.
Some DNS providers do not allow CNAME records at the domain root, requiring another supported mapping.
Validate and add the domain in App Service, then configure a TLS binding using a suitable certificate.

lessons.title: Back up and restore your App Service app
points: App Service supports restoring app content and configuration from backups; supported tiers and backup types determine available options.
Custom backups use a storage account and container. Review storage access and firewall requirements before configuring the destination.
A backup contains compressed app data and a manifest; backup schedules and retention control when copies are kept.
A full restore replaces existing content; a partial restore leaves excluded files and folders unchanged.
Automatic backups exclude linked databases. Custom backups support only specified linked database types; protect other dependencies separately and verify restore support.

lessons.title: Use Azure Application Insights
points: Application Insights is part of Azure Monitor and helps diagnose application performance and usage.
Monitor request rates, response times and failures to identify problems under load.
Track dependency calls to determine whether external services contribute to slow or failed requests.
Use exceptions, trace logs and performance counters to investigate individual failures and resource pressure.
Custom events and metrics can measure application-specific activity.

lessons.title: Exercise: Implement Web Apps
points: This optional lab requires an Azure subscription and migrates a PHP web app to App Service.
Create the web app and a staging slot, configure deployment and deploy code into staging.
Swap the tested staging deployment into production, then configure and test autoscaling.
Follow the full interactive instructions on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: App Service combines application hosting with deployment slots, security, custom domains, backups and application monitoring.

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Containers package applications and dependencies with lighter virtualization than complete virtual machines.

lessons.title: Compare containers to virtual machines
points: Containers virtualize the operating-system environment, while VMs run a complete guest operating system and kernel.
Containers generally use fewer resources and start faster. Typical process-isolated containers share the host kernel and provide a weaker security boundary than a full VM.
Container images make application packaging and deployment consistent across environments.
Use orchestration when many containers require coordinated deployment, scaling and recovery.

lessons.title: Review Azure Container Instances
points: Azure Container Instances runs containers without requiring you to manage a VM or Kubernetes cluster.
A container image packages application code, runtime, libraries, tools and settings.
Choose CPU and memory when deploying the container group. Changing its CPU, memory or GPU allocation requires deleting and recreating the group.
Container Instances supports Windows and Linux containers. Azure Files volume mounts for persistent storage are supported only for Linux containers.
A supported publicly exposed group can have an IP address and DNS name. Linux groups deployed into a virtual network use private connectivity without a public IP.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: container instances volume azure files

lessons.title: Implement container groups
points: A container group schedules containers on the same host; they share lifecycle, local networking, storage volumes and group resources. Multi-container groups support Linux only; Windows groups support one container.
Group resource requirements are calculated from the requests of its containers.
Deploy groups using ARM templates, Bicep or YAML according to the surrounding infrastructure.
For external access, expose the port at both the group IP address and the container. Containers share a port namespace, so port mapping is not supported.
Deleting a group releases its IP address and fully qualified domain name.
Separate supporting tasks into containers, such as an app plus logging, monitoring or content-update components.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: container instances container groups

lessons.title: Review Azure Container Apps
points: Azure Container Apps provides managed container hosting for APIs, microservices, background jobs and event-driven workloads.
It scales using HTTP traffic, event sources, CPU or memory, and KEDA-supported scalers; supported workloads can scale to zero.
Container Apps supports service discovery, traffic splitting and on-demand, scheduled or event-driven jobs.
It abstracts the underlying Kubernetes platform rather than exposing its Kubernetes APIs directly.
Choose Container Instances for isolated tasks, Container Apps for managed serverless microservices, or AKS when direct Kubernetes control is needed.

lessons.title: Exercise: Implement Container Instances
points: This optional exercise requires an Azure subscription.
Deploy an Azure Container Instance from a Docker image, then test and verify that the application responds.
Use the linked Microsoft Learn lab for the complete deployment instructions.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary and resources
points: Select the container platform based on isolation, orchestration and scaling needs; use container groups for cooperating containers.

paths.title: AZ-104: Monitor and back up Azure resources

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Backup planning defines recovery requirements, backup frequency, retention and access controls for important data.
Azure Backup protects supported Azure workloads and selected on-premises data.

lessons.title: What is Azure Backup?
points: Azure Backup manages backup storage and policies for supported workloads such as VMs, managed disks, file shares and databases.
Central management helps govern and monitor many protected resources.
Recovery time objective is the target time to restore service after an incident. Recovery point objective is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time.
Use encryption, access controls and deletion protection to secure backups; choose policies that meet recovery and compliance needs.

lessons.title: How Azure Backup works
points: Use the MARS agent for supported Windows files, folders and system state; DPM or Azure Backup Server can protect additional on-premises workloads.
Azure VM backup takes disk snapshots. Application- or filesystem-consistent backups use a VM extension; supported agentless backups are crash-consistent. Vaults manage recovery points and policies.
An initial full backup captures the protected data; later incremental backups transfer changed blocks. SQL database protection also supports differential and transaction-log backups.
Snapshot-tier recovery can be faster because data is near the source. Vault-standard stores an isolated copy; supported archive storage targets infrequently accessed long-term recovery points.
Choose locally, zone- or geo-redundant backup storage based on failure-protection requirements.
Backup policies define schedule and retention; enhanced VM policies support more frequent backups and selective disk protection.
Encryption, role-based access control and soft delete reduce exposure to unauthorized access and accidental deletion.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: backup azure vms introduction

lessons.title: When to use Azure Backup
points: Use Azure Backup for operational recovery from accidental deletion or corruption and for long-term compliance retention.
Choose whole-VM backup or workload-aware database backup according to what must be recovered. SQL protection supports full, differential and transaction-log backups.
Do not confuse backing up a workload across regions with restoring to a supported paired secondary region. Check the workload support matrix.
On-demand backups can use their own retention settings rather than the scheduled policy retention.
Monitor job status in vaults; reporting and workbooks help assess a wider backup estate.

lessons.title: Module assessment
points: Complete the interactive check on Microsoft Learn.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Match workload support, schedule, retention and security to the required recovery time and acceptable data loss.

modules.title: Protect your virtual machines by using Azure Backup

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Azure Backup protects VM data so that Windows and Linux workloads can be recovered after loss or corruption.
Optional practical exercises use your own Azure subscription.

lessons.title: Azure Backup features and scenarios
points: Azure Backup retains recovery points for returning to an earlier data state. Azure Site Recovery instead replicates workloads and coordinates failover.
Choose protection based on recovery time, acceptable data loss, application criticality and cost.
Azure VM backups are managed through a Recovery Services vault. Supported on-premises scenarios use MARS, Azure Backup Server or DPM.
Backup data is encrypted; role-based access control separates backup responsibilities. Customer-managed keys are available for supported configurations.
Soft delete preserves deleted backup data for recovery; enhanced soft delete can extend retention and enforce always-on protection.
Select LRS, GRS or ZRS to match the required storage failure protection.

lessons.title: Back up an Azure virtual machine by using Azure Backup
points: A Recovery Services vault manages VM recovery points, policies and access permissions.
Azure Backup takes disk snapshots on the policy schedule, then transfers changed blocks to vault storage.
Application-consistent snapshots use Windows VSS writers; Linux application consistency needs appropriate pre- and post-backup scripts.
File-system-consistent backups preserve filesystem integrity but applications may need cleanup. Crash-consistent backups omit pending memory and input/output state.
Policies set backup frequency and retention; enhanced policies support more frequent protection and selected data disks.
Snapshot recovery can be quicker than vault recovery; transfer to the vault can take time after the snapshot is created.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: backup azure vms introduction

lessons.title: Exercise - Back up an Azure virtual machine
points: This optional exercise creates Windows and Linux VMs in your own subscription, then enables Azure Backup.
Create the lab resource group and virtual network, then deploy the two VMs using Cloud Shell.
Enable backup for the Linux VM through its Backup page, select a policy and run Backup now.
For the Windows VM, create a vault with az backup vault create and enable protection with az backup protection enable-for-vm.
Start an on-demand backup with az backup protection backup-now, then inspect backup jobs and last-backup status.
Review the current interactive instructions before running commands, and clean up only the lab resources you created afterward.

lessons.title: Restore virtual machine data
points: Create a new VM to recover into another VM, or restore disks when you need to customize the recovered deployment.
Replace existing restores disks into a VM that still exists, taking a snapshot of its current disks first. It cannot replace a deleted VM.
Cross-region restore targets a supported paired secondary region; it supports creating a VM or restoring disks rather than replacing existing disks.

Cross-subscription restore uses vault-tier points for supported managed VMs in the same tenant. Restore to a subscription other than the protected VM or vault subscription requires the vault setting; ADE- and customer-key-encrypted disks are unsupported.
Cross-zonal restore has vault-redundancy and VM-support requirements. Verify the support matrix before planning it.
File recovery can mount supported backup recovery points. For Azure Disk Encryption VMs, file-level recovery and replacing the existing VM are not supported; restore the VM and copy needed files.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: backup azure arm restore vms

lessons.title: Exercise - Restore Azure virtual machine data
points: This optional exercise restores a VM protected in the preceding backup exercise.
Create a staging storage account and stop the lab VM before performing the demonstrated disk-replacement restore.
Open the VM Backup page, select Restore VM and choose an available recovery point.
Choose Replace existing and the staging location, then start the restore.
Inspect the restore job status and subtasks in Backup Jobs to confirm completion.

lessons.title: Summary
points: Test backup and restore procedures rather than assuming a successful backup proves recovery will meet requirements.
After optional labs, remove only the lab resources you created to stop unnecessary charges.

modules.title: Monitor your Azure virtual machines with Azure Monitor

lessons.title: Introduction
points: Monitor both the Azure VM host and its guest operating system, workloads and applications.
The practical steps require an Azure subscription with suitable permissions; this module specifies Contributor access.

lessons.title: Monitoring for Azure VMs
points: Metrics are numerical measurements over time; logs are timestamped events and structured records. Azure Monitor provides tools for both.
Azure automatically collects VM host metrics and activity logs. Configure Azure Monitor Agent and data collection rules for guest performance counters and event logs.
Use host metrics to track availability, CPU, disks and networking. Recommended or custom alerts notify you when monitored conditions occur.
Boot diagnostics provides screenshots and boot output for troubleshooting startup problems.
A data collection rule specifies what guest data to collect and where to send it; Log Analytics workspaces store log data for querying.

The lesson uses classic logs-based VM insights: Azure Monitor Agent collects common guest performance data into Log Analytics for curated charts and workbooks. Current monitoring also offers OpenTelemetry metrics stored in an Azure Monitor workspace.
Create additional rules for guest event logs and query them with Kusto Query Language.

lessons.title: Monitor VM host data
points: Create the lab Linux VM with recommended alert rules enabled on the Monitoring tab, and configure alert notifications.
Enable boot diagnostics with managed storage. Avoid the deprecated Linux Diagnostics Agent option in this exercise.
After deployment, inspect the default availability, CPU, disk and network graphs on the VM overview. Guest metrics require further configuration.
View Activity log for resource operations and Boot diagnostics for startup screenshots and serial output.

lessons.title: Use Metrics Explorer to view detailed host metrics
points: Open Metrics Explorer from the VM Metrics page or Azure Monitor. Choose the resource scope, namespace, metric and aggregation.
Aggregation options include count, average, minimum, maximum and sum; choose one that answers the investigation.
Add more than one metric to correlate trends, and select an appropriate time range and sampling granularity.
The example compares maximum Percentage CPU with average Inbound Flows over the last 30 minutes.

lessons.title: Collect client performance counters by using VM insights
points: The lesson demonstrates classic logs-based VM insights with a data collection rule and Log Analytics workspace. Current portal onboarding uses Monitor and Configure, with OpenTelemetry metrics selected by default and a logs-based option.
For classic logs-based monitoring, Azure Monitor Agent collects a predefined set of guest performance counters. Allow time for agent installation and data ingestion.
Confirm the agent under Extensions and applications, then inspect guest performance data.
View classic logs-based counters in VM insights performance charts and workbooks. These counters go to Log Analytics; OpenTelemetry monitoring instead stores metrics in an Azure Monitor workspace.
VM insights Map and Dependency Agent are deprecated and retire on 30 June 2028. New portal onboarding ended on 30 September 2025; do not enable them for new deployments.

lessons.title: Collect VM client event logs
points: Create a data collection rule for guest event logs; the default VM insights rule does not collect every event source.
For the Linux example, associate the VM with a Linux rule and select Linux Syslog as the data source.
Send Syslog to a Log Analytics workspace. The lesson creates a data collection endpoint, but ordinary public-endpoint Syslog collection does not require one; Private Link does.
In the VM Logs page or Azure Monitor Logs, select the appropriate scope and run a KQL query against the Syslog table.
Filter by relevant fields such as severity to investigate events associated with a performance problem.

additionalSources.title: Microsoft Learn: data collection endpoint overview

lessons.title: Summary
points: Use host metrics for platform health, VM insights for guest performance, and data collection rules plus Log Analytics for event investigation.
If you performed the optional lab, delete only its resources when finished to avoid ongoing charges.
